lesson.title: The First Cold War Showdown: The Berlin Blockade and Airlift
lesson.summary: When the Soviet Union blocked all land access to West Berlin in 1948, the United States and Britain responded with a massive airlift rather than back down, turning the divided city into the Cold War's first major crisis.
lesson.body:
After World War II the Allies had divided defeated Germany into four occupation zones controlled by the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union. Berlin, the former capital, sat entirely within the Soviet zone but was itself divided into four sectors in the same way, leaving West Berlin as an isolated island of American, British, and French control more than a hundred miles inside Soviet occupied territory. This awkward arrangement became a flashpoint once the Marshall Plan and rising tensions convinced the Western powers to move toward rebuilding, rather than punishing, their occupation zones.

In June 1948 the United States, Britain, and France introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in their combined western zones, a step toward creating a stable, self-sufficient West German economy and, eventually, an independent West German state. Stalin saw this as a direct threat to Soviet control over Germany and responded on June 24, 1948, by cutting off all road, rail, and canal access between West Germany and West Berlin, hoping to starve the city into submission and force the Western powers out entirely.

Rather than abandon the city or risk war by forcing the blockade with troops, Truman authorized an airlift. Beginning in late June 1948, American and British planes flew food, coal, and other supplies into West Berlin around the clock, landing at airfields like Tempelhof sometimes only minutes apart. The operation, which Americans called Operation Vittles, eventually involved more than two hundred thousand flights delivering over two million tons of supplies to a city of more than two million people. It was a remarkable demonstration of logistics and resolve, and it put Stalin in an impossible position: shooting down unarmed cargo planes would mean starting a war he did not want.

Stalin lifted the blockade on May 12, 1949, having failed to force the West out of Berlin or to stop the creation of an independent West German state. The crisis accelerated the very outcome Stalin had tried to prevent: the Federal Republic of Germany, commonly called West Germany, was formally established that same month, and the Soviet backed German Democratic Republic, or East Germany, followed in October 1949. Berlin itself remained divided for decades, becoming one of the most visible and dangerous symbols of the Cold War, and the crisis convinced Western leaders that they needed a permanent, formal military alliance to deter further Soviet pressure, a need that led directly to the founding of NATO.
